pos: n. (a spring and oasis on the west shore of the Dead Sea; David's refuge from Saul)
etymology: Hebrew eyn gedi, the fountain of the kid — a freshwater spring in a wilderness of salt, where wild goats came down to drink.
biblical_def: Engedi is listed among the wilderness cities of Judah (Josh 15:62). It becomes David's stronghold: “David went up from thence, and dwelt in strong holds at Engedi” (1Sa 23:29), and Saul followed — “Behold, David is in the wilderness of Engedi” (1Sa 24:1). In the cave there David spared the king and told his men why: “The LORD forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, the LORD'S anointed” (1Sa 24:6). Generations later an invading host camps at the same place (2Ch 20:2), and the Song makes it a picture of sweetness: “My beloved is unto me as a cluster of camphire in the vineyards of Engedi” (Son 1:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an oasis as a fertile spot in a sandy desert, and a fountain as a spring or source of water issuing from the earth.
webster_full: OASIS, n. A fertile spot in a sandy desert, where there is water and verdure.
FOUNTAIN, n. A spring, or source of water; properly, a spring or issuing of water from the earth.
STRONGHOLD, n. A fastness; a fort or fortress; a place of security.
scriptures: And Nibshan, and the city of Salt, and Engedi; six cities with their villages.
And David went up from thence, and dwelt in strong holds at Engedi.
And he said unto his men, The LORD forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, the LORD'S anointed, to stretch forth mine hand against him, seeing he is the anointed of the LORD.
My beloved is unto me as a cluster of camphire in the vineyards of Engedi.
corruption_summary: David had the anointed king at the end of his blade and would not take the crown a year early, because the throne was God's to give.
corruption_paragraphs: The cave at Engedi is the hardest test David ever passed. Saul was hunting him without cause, had already murdered the priests of Nob, and walked alone into the very cave where David's men were hiding. They read the providence as permission — behold the day of which the LORD said unto thee. David read it as a temptation. He cut the skirt of the robe and his heart smote him even for that, and he gave the reason twice: the LORD forbid, seeing he is the anointed of the LORD. He had been anointed himself, by Samuel, years before; he simply would not take by his own hand what God had promised to give.

The corruption to name is the reading of opportunity as calling. An open door is not by itself a command, and the men in the cave had a plausible theology of the moment: God has arranged this, therefore God intends it. Scripture is full of counterexamples — Abraham and Hagar, Saul and the sacrifice at Gilgal, Uzzah and the ark — where an evident need and an evident means combined to produce a sin. The test of an action is never the convenience of the circumstances but the revealed will of God, and at Engedi that will was the sixth commandment and the office of the LORD's anointed.
roots_summary: Hebrew ayin (H5869), a spring or eye; gedi (H1423), a kid; mashiach (H4899), anointed one.
roots_lines: Hebrew ayin (H5869) — spring, fountain, eye; Joshua 15:62, Genesis 16:7.
Hebrew gedi (H1423) — a kid, young goat; Genesis 38:17, Judges 6:19.
Hebrew mashiach (H4899) — anointed; 1 Samuel 24:6, 26:9, Psalm 2:2.
Hebrew metsad (H4679) — stronghold, fastness; 1 Samuel 23:29, 24:22.
Hebrew kopher (H3724) — camphire, henna; Song of Solomon 1:14, 4:13.
usage: “David… dwelt in strong holds at Engedi” — a spring in a wilderness of salt.
“The LORD forbid… seeing he is the anointed of the LORD” — the cave refused.
“A cluster of camphire in the vineyards of Engedi” — the Song's figure.

pos: n. (a fortress city commanding the Jezreel valley; long left in Canaanite hands, and the place where Saul's body was hung)
etymology: Hebrew beyth shean, house of quiet or house of security — a name of ease for a city that guarded the junction of two valleys and could not be taken.
biblical_def: The house of Joseph complains that the good ground is held against them: “all the Canaanites that dwell in the land of the valley have chariots of iron, both they who are of Bethshean and her towns, and they who are of the valley of Jezreel” (Josh 17:16). Joshua answers with a command and a promise: “thou shalt drive out the Canaanites, though they have iron chariots, and though they be strong” (Josh 17:18). Chronicles lists it in Manasseh's allotment (1Ch 7:29), and only under Solomon does it appear as an administered district: “all Bethshean, which is by Zartanah beneath Jezreel” (1Ki 4:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chariot as a car or vehicle used formerly in war, and a valley as a hollow or low tract of land between hills or mountains.
webster_full: CHARIOT, n. A half coach; a car or vehicle used formerly in war, drawn by two or more horses.
VALLEY, n. A hollow or low tract of land between hills or mountains.
FORTRESS, n. Any fortified place; a fort; a castle; a strong hold.
scriptures: And the children of Joseph said, The hill is not enough for us: and all the Canaanites that dwell in the land of the valley have chariots of iron, both they who are of Bethshean and her towns, and they who are of the valley of Jezreel.

But the mountain shall be thine; for it is a wood, and thou shalt cut it down: and the outgoings of it shall be thine: for thou shalt drive out the Canaanites, though they have iron chariots, and though they be strong.
And by the borders of the children of Manasseh, Bethshean and her towns, Taanach and her towns, Megiddo and her towns, Dor and her towns. In these dwelt the children of Joseph the son of Israel.
Baana the son of Ahilud; to him pertained Taanach and Megiddo, and all Bethshean, which is by Zartanah beneath Jezreel, from Bethshean to Abelmeholah, even unto the place that is beyond Jokneam:
corruption_summary: Joshua answers a complaint about iron chariots with a command to go and take the valley, and the tribe that complained never did.
corruption_paragraphs: Joshua 17 is a conversation between a tribe and its leader, and the tribe loses the argument twice. The children of Joseph say the hill country is too small; Joshua tells them to clear the wood. They say the valley is impossible because of iron chariots; Joshua tells them the outgoings shall be theirs, for thou shalt drive out the Canaanites, though they have iron chariots, and though they be strong. Every objection is answered with a promise attached to a labour. Judges 1:27 records the result: Manasseh did not drive out the inhabitants of Bethshean. The word of God about the chariots was true, and it was never tested.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a divine promise usually arrives as a command. Israel is told the land is given — and told to go up and take it, city by city, with the strong cities left for last and the iron chariots left standing in the valleys. The believer's sanctification runs the same way in Philippians 2:12-13: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do. The Canaanites in the valley are not left there by an oversight of providence. They are left there to be driven out.
roots_summary: Hebrew beyth (H1004), house; shean, quiet, ease; rekeb barzel, chariots of iron; yarash (H3423), to dispossess.
roots_lines: Hebrew beyth (H1004) — house, place; Joshua 17:16, Genesis 28:19.
Hebrew rekeb (H7393) — chariot, chariotry; Joshua 17:16, Judges 4:3.
Hebrew barzel (H1270) — iron; Joshua 17:18, Deuteronomy 8:9.
Hebrew yarash (H3423) — to drive out, dispossess; Joshua 17:18, Numbers 33:53.
Hebrew emeq (H6010) — valley, vale; Joshua 17:16, Genesis 14:17.
usage: “Chariots of iron… of Bethshean and her towns” — the objection raised.
“Thou shalt drive out the Canaanites, though they have iron chariots” — the answer.
“All Bethshean, which is by Zartanah beneath Jezreel” — Solomon's district.

pos: n. (a place near Bethel; and in Hosea, a name of contempt substituted for Bethel itself)
etymology: Hebrew beyth aven, house of vanity or house of iniquity — a deliberate parody of beyth el, house of God. Hosea does not misname the town; he renames it for what was in it.
biblical_def: As a landmark Bethaven is ordinary: Ai lay “beside Bethaven, on the east side of Bethel” (Josh 7:2); the Philistines “pitched in Michmash, eastward from Bethaven” (1Sa 13:5); and after Jonathan's victory, “the LORD saved Israel that day: and the battle passed over unto Bethaven” (1Sa 14:23). Then Hosea turns the name into an indictment: “come not ye unto Gilgal, neither go ye up to Bethaven, nor swear, The LORD liveth” (Hos 4:15), and again — “The inhabitants of Samaria shall fear because of the calves of Bethaven” (Hos 10:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vanity as emptiness, want of substance to satisfy desire, and iniquity as a deviation from rectitude; injustice; wickedness.
webster_full: VANITY, n. Emptiness; want of substance to satisfy desire; uncertainty; inanity.
INIQUITY, n. Injustice; unrighteousness; a deviation from rectitude; want of equity.
IDOL, n. An image, form or representation, usually of a man or other animal, consecrated as an object of worship.
scriptures: And Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai, which is beside Bethaven, on the east side of Bethel, and spake unto them, saying, Go up and view the country. And the men went up and viewed Ai.
So the LORD saved Israel that day: and the battle passed over unto Bethaven.
Though thou, Israel, play the harlot, yet let not Judah offend; and come not ye unto Gilgal, neither go ye up to Bethaven, nor swear, The LORD liveth.

The inhabitants of Samaria shall fear because of the calves of Bethaven: for the people thereof shall mourn over it, and the priests thereof that rejoiced on it, for the glory thereof, because it is departed from it.
corruption_summary: Hosea will not call Bethel the house of God while a golden calf stands in it, and renames it the house of vanity.
corruption_paragraphs: Bethel was holy ground by history: Jacob's ladder, the pillar, the vow, the name given by God Himself — house of God. Jeroboam put a golden calf there and said, behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt. He did not propose a new religion; he proposed a convenient version of the true one, with the LORD's name still on it. Hosea's answer is to refuse the name. It is Bethaven now, the house of vanity, and its calves are what the people of Samaria will mourn over when the glory departs. A place does not keep its title by its history.

The corruption to name is worship of the true God by means He has not appointed, which is the second commandment's specific concern and the whole substance of Jeroboam's sin. It is not atheism and it is not open idolatry; it is convenience wearing the covenant name, and the men who practise it are usually sincere. Hosea 4:15 forbids even the oath — nor swear, The LORD liveth — in that place, because a true name attached to a false worship compounds rather than sanctifies. The regulative principle exists to keep churches from becoming Bethaven while the sign over the door still reads Bethel.
roots_summary: Hebrew aven (H205), vanity, iniquity, trouble; beyth el, house of God; egel (H5695), calf.
roots_lines: Hebrew aven (H205) — vanity, iniquity, wickedness; Hosea 4:15, 10:5, Isaiah 1:13.
Hebrew beyth el — house of God, Bethel; Genesis 28:19, Joshua 7:2.
Hebrew egel (H5695) — calf; Hosea 10:5, Exodus 32:4, 1 Kings 12:28.
Hebrew kabod (H3519) — glory; Hosea 10:5, 1 Samuel 4:21.
Hebrew shaba (H7650) — to swear, take an oath; Hosea 4:15, Deuteronomy 6:13.
usage: “Ai, which is beside Bethaven, on the east side of Bethel” — the ordinary landmark.
“Neither go ye up to Bethaven, nor swear, The LORD liveth” — the name refused.
“The calves of Bethaven” — what Samaria will mourn.

pos: n. (the Moabite idol of Mount Peor, and the apostasy of Israel joined to it on the edge of the promised land)
etymology: Hebrew baal peor, lord of Peor — the local Baal of the mountain where Balaam had blessed Israel three times. The idol takes its name from the very ground where the curse had failed.
biblical_def: “And Israel joined himself unto Baalpeor: and the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel” (Num 25:3), the sin having begun with the daughters of Moab (Num 25:1) and ending in a plague in which “those that died… were twenty and four thousand” (Num 25:9). Moses commanded the judges, “Slay ye every one his men that were joined unto Baalpeor” (Num 25:5), and afterwards reminded the next generation: “all the men that followed Baalpeor, the LORD thy God hath destroyed them from among you” (Deu 4:3). Hosea remembers it as the turning point: “they went to Baalpeor, and separated themselves unto that shame” (Hos 9:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Baal as an idol among the ancient Chaldeans and Syrians, and notes the word signifies lord, master, or possessor.
webster_full: BAAL, n. An idol among the ancient Chaldeans and Syrians, representing the sun. The word signifies lord or commander.
IDOLATRY, n. The worship of idols, images, or any thing made by hands, or which is not God.
APOSTASY, n. An abandonment of what one has professed; a total desertion, or departure from one's faith or religion.
scriptures: And Israel abode in Shittim, and the people began to commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab.
And Israel joined himself unto Baalpeor: and the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel.
Your eyes have seen what the LORD did because of Baalpeor: for all the men that followed Baalpeor, the LORD thy God hath destroyed them from among you.

I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness; I saw your fathers as the firstripe in the fig tree at her first time: but they went to Baalpeor, and separated themselves unto that shame; and their abominations were according as they loved.
corruption_summary: Balaam could not curse Israel with words and destroyed twenty-four thousand of them with a counsel, and Revelation names the tactic by his name.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 22 through 24 is a comedy of failed cursing: three times Balaam opens his mouth to curse and blessing comes out, and he tells Balak plainly that he cannot go beyond the word of the LORD. Numbers 25 is what happened next, and Numbers 31:16 supplies the missing link — these caused the children of Israel, through the counsel of Balaam, to commit trespass against the LORD in the matter of Peor. What the enemy could not do by opposition he did by invitation. Christ names the doctrine of Balaam to the church at Pergamos in Revelation 2:14 as a live danger to a congregation that had already withstood persecution.

The corruption to name is seduction as the church's chief peril, which the New Testament assumes and modern Christians frequently do not. Congregations brace for hostility and are undone by hospitality; the daughters of Moab invited Israel to sacrifices and the people ate and bowed down. Paul cites this very episode in 1 Corinthians 10:8 as an example written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come, and draws the conclusion in the next verses: wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall. Peor is on the border of Canaan. The failure came within sight of the promise.
roots_summary: Hebrew baal (H1168), lord, the Canaanite deity; Peor (H6465), the mountain; tsamad (H6775), to be joined, yoked together.
roots_lines: Hebrew baal (H1168) — Baal, lord, master; Numbers 25:3, Judges 2:13, 1 Kings 18:21.
Hebrew Peor (H6465) — Peor, the mount; Numbers 23:28, 25:18.
Hebrew tsamad (H6775) — to join, be yoked to; Numbers 25:3, 25:5, Psalm 106:28.
Hebrew zanah (H2181) — to commit whoredom; Numbers 25:1, Hosea 4:15.
Hebrew bosheth (H1322) — shame; Hosea 9:10, Jeremiah 3:24.
usage: “Israel joined himself unto Baalpeor” — on the edge of the land.
“All the men that followed Baalpeor, the LORD thy God hath destroyed them.”
“They… separated themselves unto that shame” — Hosea's memory of it.

pos: n. (the older name of Bethlehem and of its district; the name under which Micah announced the birthplace of Messiah)
etymology: Hebrew ephrathah, fruitfulness. Genesis glosses it directly: Ephrath, which is Bethlehem — two names, fruitfulness and house of bread, for one small town in Judah.
biblical_def: Rachel died there: “Rachel died, and was buried in the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem” (Gen 35:19). The genealogies keep the name: Hur, “the firstborn of Ephratah, the father of Bethlehem” (1Ch 4:4). A psalm of the ark uses it: “Lo, we heard of it at Ephratah: we found it in the fields of the wood” (Psa 132:6). And Micah makes it the address of the incarnation: “But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting” (Mic 5:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fruitful as producing fruit in abundance, prolific, and notes the figurative sense of that which is productive of good.
webster_full: FRUITFUL, a. Producing fruit in abundance; as fruitful soil; a fruitful tree.
FRUITFUL, a. Productive of any thing; producing in abundance; as a fruitful land.
NATIVITY, n. Birth; the coming into life or the world.
scriptures: And Rachel died, and was buried in the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem.
And Penuel the father of Gedor, and Ezer the father of Hushah. These are the sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephratah, the father of Bethlehem.
Lo, we heard of it at Ephratah: we found it in the fields of the wood.

But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.
corruption_summary: Micah 5:2 names both the town where Christ was born and the eternity from which He came, in one sentence.
corruption_paragraphs: Micah 5:2 is one of the great Christological texts of the Old Testament because it holds two things together that no mere man could hold. The ruler of Israel comes forth out of Bethlehem Ephratah, a real birth in a real village too small to be counted among the thousands of Judah — and His goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting. A true and complete humanity with a beginning in time, and a true and complete deity without beginning at all. Chalcedon states in careful Greek what Micah had already said in a single Hebrew verse, and the chief priests quoted the first half of it to Herod without appearing to notice the second.

The corruption to name is every Christology that keeps one clause and drops the other. Arianism and its modern descendants keep Bethlehem and lose from everlasting, making the Son a creature however exalted. Docetism and its quieter evangelical version keep the eternity and lose the flesh, leaving a Christ who seemed to be a man and did not truly hunger, weep, or die. Micah refuses both, and so does the church that confesses one Person in two natures, without confusion, change, division, or separation. The smallness of the town is part of the doctrine: God chose the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty.
roots_summary: Hebrew Ephrathah (H672), fruitfulness; beyth lechem, house of bread; motsaah (H4163), goings forth, origins.
roots_lines: Hebrew Ephrathah (H672) — Ephratah, fruitfulness; Genesis 35:19, Ruth 4:11, Micah 5:2.
Hebrew beyth lechem — Bethlehem, house of bread; Genesis 35:19, 1 Samuel 16:1.
Hebrew motsaah (H4163) — goings forth, origin; Micah 5:2, 2 Kings 10:27.
Hebrew olam (H5769) — everlasting, of old; Micah 5:2, Psalm 90:2.
Hebrew moshel (H4910) — ruler, one who has dominion; Micah 5:2, Genesis 45:8.
usage: “Ephrath, which is Bethlehem” — Genesis glossing the older name.
“Thou be little among the thousands of Judah” — and the ruler comes from there.
“Whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.”

pos: n. (a town on the plain of Sharon; where Peter healed Aeneas and the whole district turned to the Lord)
etymology: Greek form of the Hebrew Lod, a town of Benjamin rebuilt after the return. It lay on the road from Jerusalem to Joppa, which is why Peter was near enough to be sent for.
biblical_def: “And it came to pass, as Peter passed throughout all quarters, he came down also to the saints which dwelt at Lydda” (Act 9:32). There he found Aeneas, eight years bedridden: “Aeneas, Jesus Christ maketh thee whole: arise, and make thy bed. And he arose immediately” (Act 9:34). The effect was regional: “all that dwelt at Lydda and Saron saw him, and turned to the Lord” (Act 9:35). And the town's position brought Peter to Joppa: “forasmuch as Lydda was nigh to Joppa… they sent unto him two men, desiring him that he would not delay to come to them” (Act 9:38).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a saint as a person sanctified; a holy or godly person; one eminent for piety and virtue — and in Scripture, a believer in Christ.
webster_full: SAINT, n. A person sanctified; a holy or godly person; one eminent for piety and virtue.
SAINT, n. In Scripture, the sanctified, or those who are called and set apart; believers in Christ.
PALSY, n. The loss or defect of the power of voluntary muscular motion in the whole body, or in a particular part.
scriptures: And it came to pass, as Peter passed throughout all quarters, he came down also to the saints which dwelt at Lydda.
And Peter said unto him, Aeneas, Jesus Christ maketh thee whole: arise, and make thy bed. And he arose immediately.
And all that dwelt at Lydda and Saron saw him, and turned to the Lord.
And forasmuch as Lydda was nigh to Joppa, and the disciples had heard that Peter was there, they sent unto him two men, desiring him that he would not delay to come to them.
corruption_summary: Peter's words to Aeneas name the healer and it is not Peter, which is the settled apostolic pattern.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 9:34 is a model of apostolic speech: Aeneas, Jesus Christ maketh thee whole. Peter does not say I heal thee and does not say be healed; he announces the agent. It is the same care he shows at the Beautiful Gate, where the crowd runs together in amazement and Peter asks, why look ye so earnestly on us, as though by our own power or holiness we had made this man to walk? And the same care Paul and Barnabas show at Lystra, tearing their clothes and crying, we also are men of like passions with you. The apostolic miracles authenticate a message about Christ, and their bearers are careful never to stand in the light.

The corruption to name is the transfer of glory from Christ to the man He works through, which every generation of the church has managed to arrange. Lydda gives the corrective in the result rather than in a rebuke: they saw Aeneas walking and turned to the Lord — not to Peter, who was passing through, and who left shortly for Joppa when two men came asking. The healed man's first instruction is domestic and unglamorous: arise, and make thy bed. Restoration in Scripture returns a man to ordinary duty rather than to a platform.
roots_summary: Greek Ludda (G3069), Lydda; Saron (G4565), the plain of Sharon; iaomai (G2390), to heal, make whole.
roots_lines: Greek Ludda (G3069) — Lydda; Acts 9:32, 9:35, 9:38 only.
Greek Saron (G4565) — Sharon, the coastal plain; Acts 9:35 only.
Greek iaomai (G2390) — to heal, make whole; Acts 9:34, Luke 9:11.
Greek paralelumenos (G3886) — palsied, paralyzed; Acts 9:33, Luke 5:18.
Greek epistrepho (G1994) — to turn, be converted; Acts 9:35, 1 Thessalonians 1:9.
usage: “The saints which dwelt at Lydda” — a church already there before Peter arrived.
“Aeneas, Jesus Christ maketh thee whole” — the healer named.
“All that dwelt at Lydda and Saron… turned to the Lord.”

pos: n. (a hill town of Judah; fortified by Rehoboam and rebuilt after the exile)
etymology: Hebrew beyth tsur, house of rock — a name from the ridge it stood on, south of Jerusalem on the road to Hebron.
biblical_def: Bethzur appears in Judah's hill-country allotment: “Halhul, Bethzur, and Gedor” (Josh 15:58), and in the genealogy of Caleb's line: “Maon was the father of Bethzur” (1Ch 2:45). Rehoboam made it one of his defended cities: “And Bethzur, and Shoco, and Adullam” (2Ch 11:7). And after the exile its ruler took a share of the wall: “After him repaired Nehemiah the son of Azbuk, the ruler of the half part of Bethzur, unto the place over against the sepulchres of David” (Neh 3:16), the Levites repairing next to him (Neh 3:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a rock as a large mass of stony matter, and figuratively defense, means of safety, protection, strength.
webster_full: ROCK, n. A large mass of stony matter, usually compounded of two or more simple minerals.
ROCK, n. In Scripture, defense; means of safety; protection; strength; asylum.
REPAIR, v.t. To restore to a sound or good state after decay, injury or partial destruction.
scriptures: And the son of Shammai was Maon: and Maon was the father of Bethzur.
And Bethzur, and Shoco, and Adullam,

After him repaired Nehemiah the son of Azbuk, the ruler of the half part of Bethzur, unto the place over against the sepulchres of David, and to the pool that was made, and unto the house of the mighty.
corruption_summary: Nehemiah 3 is a list of names against sections of wall, and the Holy Spirit thought the assignment of ordinary men worth recording.
corruption_paragraphs: Nehemiah 3 is one of the least quoted and most encouraging chapters in the Old Testament. It is a register: the high priest and his brethren built the sheep gate; the men of Jericho built next to them; the goldsmiths, the apothecaries, the merchants, the Levites, the rulers of half-districts like Bethzur, each with a named length of wall. Some are noted for building over against their own house. One family is noted for refusing — the nobles of Tekoa put not their necks to the work of their Lord. The wall went up in fifty-two days because a hundred small assignments were kept, and the record of who kept them is Scripture.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God keeps the register. First Corinthians 3:8 says every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labour; Hebrews 6:10 says God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love; Malachi 3:16 describes a book of remembrance written before Him for them that feared the LORD. The ruler of half Bethzur repaired a stretch of wall by the sepulchres of David and is named for it two and a half thousand years later. Faithfulness in a small assigned section is the ordinary shape of Christian service, and it is not anonymous.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsur (H6697), rock, cliff, and figuratively God as refuge; chazaq (H2388), to repair, strengthen; pelek (H6418), district, part.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsur (H6697) — rock, strength, refuge; Joshua 15:58, Deuteronomy 32:4, Psalm 18:2.
Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to repair, make strong; Nehemiah 3:16, 3:17.
Hebrew pelek (H6418) — district, part, portion; Nehemiah 3:16, 3:12.
Hebrew qeber (H6913) — grave, sepulchre; Nehemiah 3:16, Genesis 23:6.
Hebrew metsurah (H4694) — fortification, stronghold; 2 Chronicles 11:5, 11:10.
usage: “Halhul, Bethzur, and Gedor” — the hill country of Judah.
“And Bethzur, and Shoco, and Adullam” — Rehoboam's defended cities.
“The ruler of the half part of Bethzur” — named for his stretch of wall.

pos: n. (a spring outside Jerusalem on the border of Judah and Benjamin; the meeting place of two conspiracies)
etymology: Hebrew eyn rogel, the fuller's fountain — the spring where cloth was trodden clean. It lay just below the city, out of sight of the walls, which is why it kept being chosen for business that could not be done inside.
biblical_def: Enrogel is first a boundary marker, where the tribal line descends past the valley of Hinnom (Josh 18:16). Then it becomes a listening post: during Absalom's revolt, “Jonathan and Ahimaaz stayed by Enrogel; for they might not be seen to come into the city: and a wench went and told them; and they went and told king David” (2Sa 17:17) — and the warning they carried saved him: “Arise, and pass quickly over the water: for thus hath Ahithophel counselled against you” (2Sa 17:21). And it is where the last of David's sons tried to seize the throne: “Adonijah slew sheep and oxen and fat cattle by the stone of Zoheleth, which is by Enrogel” (1Ki 1:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a fuller as one whose occupation is to full cloth, and a fountain as a spring or source of water issuing from the earth.
webster_full: FULLER, n. One whose occupation is to full cloth; that is, to cleanse and thicken it.
FOUNTAIN, n. A spring, or source of water; properly, a spring or issuing of water from the earth.
CONSPIRACY, n. A combination of men for an evil purpose; an agreement between two or more persons to commit some crime in concert.
scriptures: And the border came down to the end of the mountain that lieth before the valley of the son of Hinnom, and which is in the valley of the giants on the north, and descended to the valley of Hinnom, to the side of Jebusi on the south, and descended to Enrogel,
Now Jonathan and Ahimaaz stayed by Enrogel; for they might not be seen to come into the city: and a wench went and told them; and they went and told king David.

And it came to pass, after they were departed, that they came up out of the well, and went and told king David, and said unto David, Arise, and pass quickly over the water: for thus hath Ahithophel counselled against you.
And Adonijah slew sheep and oxen and fat cattle by the stone of Zoheleth, which is by Enrogel, and called all his brethren the king's sons, and all the men of Judah the king's servants:
corruption_summary: Adonijah invited everyone who would say yes and left out Nathan, Benaiah and Solomon, which is how a false claim always assembles its support.
corruption_paragraphs: First Kings 1 records the guest list twice, once for who was called and once for who was not: he called all his brethren the king's sons and all the men of Judah the king's servants; but Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah, and the mighty men, and Solomon his brother, he called not. A feast at Enrogel with a full table and a careful set of exclusions. The chapter earlier gives the root: his father had not displeased him at any time in saying, Why hast thou done so? An unrebuked son grew into a man who assembled a coronation out of everyone who would agree with him.

The corruption to name is the selection of counsel for agreement, which Scripture treats as a mark of the fool rather than a strategy of the wise. Proverbs is relentless on it: in the multitude of counsellors there is safety; he that hearkeneth unto counsel is wise; a fool hath no delight in understanding, but that his heart may discover itself. Rehoboam did the same thing at Shechem and lost ten tribes. Adonijah's feast at Enrogel was still in progress when the sound of Solomon's trumpet reached it, and the guests rose up and every man went his way. Support gathered by exclusion evaporates on contact with the truth.
roots_summary: Hebrew ayin (H5869), spring, fountain; ragal (H7270), to go about on foot, to spy; Zocheleth (H2120), the serpent stone.
roots_lines: Hebrew ayin (H5869) — spring, fountain, eye; Joshua 18:16, 15:7.
Hebrew ragal (H7270) — to go on foot, spy out, slander; Joshua 15:7, 2 Samuel 19:27.
Hebrew Zocheleth (H2120) — the stone of Zoheleth; 1 Kings 1:9 only.
Hebrew etsah (H6098) — counsel, advice; 2 Samuel 17:21, Proverbs 11:14.
Hebrew gey ben hinnom — valley of the son of Hinnom; Joshua 18:16, Jeremiah 7:31.
usage: “Jonathan and Ahimaaz stayed by Enrogel; for they might not be seen” — David's couriers.
“Arise, and pass quickly over the water” — the warning that saved the king.
“By the stone of Zoheleth, which is by Enrogel” — Adonijah's feast.

pos: n. (a town on the Judah-Benjamin border in the desert of the Jordan valley)
etymology: Hebrew beyth ha-arabah, house of the desert plain — from arabah, the arid rift that runs from the sea of Chinnereth down past the Dead Sea.
biblical_def: Betharabah stands on a boundary line and is named three times in Joshua, twice on each side of it. In the border description of Judah: “the border went up to Bethhogla, and passed along by the north of Betharabah” (Josh 15:6). In Judah's wilderness cities: “In the wilderness, Betharabah, Middin, and Secacah” (Josh 15:61). And in Benjamin's allotment: “And Betharabah, and Zemaraim, and Bethel” (Josh 18:22). The same chapter that lists Judah's inheritance also records what Judah could not take: “the children of Judah could not drive them out: but the Jebusites dwell with the children of Judah at Jerusalem unto this day” (Josh 15:63).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a desert as an uninhabited tract of land, a region in its natural state, and a border as the outer edge or boundary of any thing.
webster_full: DESERT, n. An uninhabited tract of land; a region in its natural state; a wilderness; a solitude.
BORDER, n. The outer edge of any thing; the extreme part or surrounding line; the confine or exterior limit of a country.
INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession; that which is or may be inherited.
scriptures: And the border went up to Bethhogla, and passed along by the north of Betharabah; and the border went up to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben:
In the wilderness, Betharabah, Middin, and Secacah,
As for the Jebusites the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the children of Judah could not drive them out: but the Jebusites dwell with the children of Judah at Jerusalem unto this day.
And Betharabah, and Zemaraim, and Bethel,
corruption_summary: The land was divided by exact survey before it was fully possessed, so the boundary lists are a record of promise rather than of achievement.
corruption_paragraphs: Joshua 15 to 19 is one of the longest stretches of unbroken geography in Scripture, and readers regularly skip it. The chapters are a land registry: every tribe, every border, every town, drawn by lot before the ground was cleared. Judah's list includes Jerusalem, which Judah could not take — the Jebusites dwell with the children of Judah unto this day. The survey was accurate and the possession was partial, and both facts are recorded in the same chapter without embarrassment. God's allotment does not wait on Israel's success, and Israel's failure does not shrink the map.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the believer's inheritance is deeded before it is enjoyed. Ephesians 1:11 says in whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will; 1 Peter 1:4 calls it incorruptible, undefiled, and reserved in heaven. Meanwhile there are Jebusites in the city. The boundary lists in Joshua exist so that a discouraged Israelite could read exactly what was his while looking at ground he had not yet walked, which is the position of every Christian this side of glory.
roots_summary: Hebrew arabah (H6160), desert plain, the Jordan rift; gebul (H1366), border, boundary; nachalah (H5159), inheritance.
roots_lines: Hebrew arabah (H6160) — desert plain, wilderness; Joshua 15:6, Deuteronomy 1:1, Isaiah 35:1.
Hebrew gebul (H1366) — border, boundary, territory; Joshua 15:6, Psalm 74:17.
Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — inheritance, possession; Joshua 18:20, Psalm 16:6.
Hebrew goral (H1486) — lot; Joshua 18:11, Proverbs 16:33.
Hebrew yarash (H3423) — to drive out, take possession; Joshua 15:63, 17:18.
usage: “Passed along by the north of Betharabah” — a line drawn in the desert.
“In the wilderness, Betharabah, Middin, and Secacah” — Judah's desert towns.
“The children of Judah could not drive them out” — the same chapter, honestly.

pos: n. (spring of gardens; the name of two towns, one of them given to the Levites)
etymology: Hebrew eyn gannim, fountain of gardens — a name that describes what a spring makes of the ground around it.
biblical_def: One Engannim lies in the lowland of Judah: “And Zanoah, and Engannim, Tappuah, and Enam” (Josh 15:34). The other is in Issachar: “And Remeth, and Engannim, and Enhaddah, and Bethpazzez” (Josh 19:21), and it is set apart for the sons of Gershon: “Jarmuth with her suburbs, Engannim with her suburbs; four cities” (Josh 21:29). That allotment belongs to a larger arrangement: “All the cities of the Levites within the possession of the children of Israel were forty and eight cities with their suburbs” (Josh 21:41).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a garden as a piece of ground appropriated to the cultivation of herbs, fruits and flowers, and suburbs as the parts adjacent to a city.
webster_full: GARDEN, n. A piece of ground appropriated to the cultivation of herbs, or plants, fruits and flowers.
SUBURB, n. A building without the walls of a city, but near them; more generally, the parts adjacent to a city or town.
LEVITE, n. One of the tribe or family of Levi; a descendant of Levi; more particularly, an officer in the Jewish church.
scriptures: And Zanoah, and Engannim, Tappuah, and Enam,
And Remeth, and Engannim, and Enhaddah, and Bethpazzez;
Jarmuth with her suburbs, Engannim with her suburbs; four cities.
All the cities of the Levites within the possession of the children of Israel were forty and eight cities with their suburbs.
corruption_summary: Levi got no territory and forty-eight towns scattered through every other tribe, so that the teaching order lived where the people lived.
corruption_paragraphs: Joshua 21 completes a design begun in Genesis 49. Jacob had said of Simeon and Levi that he would divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel — spoken as a judgment for the violence at Shechem. In Levi's case the scattering became a vocation. The tribe received no block of land but forty-eight cities with their suburbs, distributed through every other inheritance, six of them cities of refuge. Deuteronomy 33:10 gives the purpose: they shall teach Jacob thy judgments, and Israel thy law. A curse became the mechanism by which every tribe had teachers of the law inside its own borders.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's ministers are meant to live among the people they teach. The Levitical cities were not a compound; they were forty-eight ordinary towns, each with pasture around it, in the middle of everyone else's inheritance. Malachi 2:7 states the office: the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth. And the LORD Himself was Levi's portion, which is the other half of the arrangement — a tribe with no estate, dependent on tithes and on God, teaching the tribes that had estates.
roots_summary: Hebrew ayin (H5869), spring; gan / gannim (H1588), garden, gardens; migrash (H4054), suburbs, common land around a city.
roots_lines: Hebrew ayin (H5869) — spring, fountain; Joshua 15:34, 19:21.
Hebrew gan (H1588) — garden; Genesis 2:8, Song of Solomon 4:12.
Hebrew migrash (H4054) — suburbs, open pasture land; Joshua 21:29, 21:41, Numbers 35:2.
Hebrew Gereshon (H1648) — Gershon, son of Levi; Joshua 21:27, Exodus 6:16.
Hebrew cheleq (H2506) — portion, share; Deuteronomy 10:9, Numbers 18:20.
usage: “Engannim with her suburbs; four cities” — a Levitical town in Issachar.
“Forty and eight cities with their suburbs” — the whole Levitical portion.
“Zanoah, and Engannim, Tappuah, and Enam” — the other town, in Judah.
